proposal.hypothesis: Under the catalog's Gaussian-error and simplified transit assumptions, expanding the field boundary by one cross-track standard deviation will reduce missed true crossings compared with the nominal field plus the unchanged +/-5-second temporal window, while increasing false-positive alerts. Measure both outcomes separately for fresh and stale scenarios. Field expansion is an explicit paper suggestion; the one-sigma prescription and distributional assumptions are agent-generated.

evidence.quote: If we assume a cross-track error of 500 m then the expected angular error for a low altitude object (335 km) at zenith (worst case) is 0.09 degree (5.2 arcminutes).
This is diﬃcult to mitigate and will have a larger real eﬀect on smaller ﬁelds.

proposal.hypothesis: Under the fixed catalog assumptions, a two-sigma cross-track guard will reduce missed true crossings further than the one-sigma guard but increase false-positive alerts. Compare both guards with the common nominal-field control using matched simulated candidates, reporting missed-crossing fractions, false-positive counts and uncertainty separately for fresh and stale scenarios. Neither the two-sigma choice nor its operational desirability is established by the paper.
proposal.title: Measure the tradeoff from a two-sigma guard

evidence.quote: For example an in-track error of 25 km (Vallado & Cefola 2012) will lead to an angular oﬀset of 4.3 degrees or 3.26 seconds.

proposal.hypothesis: With the temporal window fixed at +/-5 seconds, a three-sigma cross-track guard will reduce spatial misses relative to the nominal control but leave more residual timing-related misses in the stale scenario than in the fresh scenario. Compare against the two-sigma guard to measure incremental recovery and added false positives; distinguish spatial and temporal causes where raw outputs permit. This is an agent hypothesis about the prescribed simulation, not evidence of real-world coverage or novelty.

proposals.hypothesis: Under the catalog's Gaussian-error and simplified transit assumptions, expanding the field boundary by one cross-track standard deviation will reduce missed true crossings compared with the nominal field plus the unchanged +/-5-second temporal window, while increasing false-positive alerts. Measure both outcomes separately for fresh and stale scenarios. Field expansion is an explicit paper suggestion; the one-sigma prescription and distributional assumptions are agent-generated.

evidence.quote: For example an in-track error of 25 km (Vallado & Cefola 2012) will lead to an angular oﬀset of 4.3 degrees or 3.26 seconds.

proposals.hypothesis: With the temporal window fixed at +/-5 seconds, a three-sigma cross-track guard will reduce spatial misses relative to the nominal control but leave more residual timing-related misses in the stale scenario than in the fresh scenario. Compare against the two-sigma guard to measure incremental recovery and added false positives; distinguish spatial and temporal causes where raw outputs permit. This is an agent hypothesis about the prescribed simulation, not evidence of real-world coverage or novelty.

proposals.hypothesis: Under the fixed catalog assumptions, a two-sigma cross-track guard will reduce missed true crossings further than the one-sigma guard but increase false-positive alerts. Compare both guards with the common nominal-field control using matched simulated candidates, reporting missed-crossing fractions, false-positive counts and uncertainty separately for fresh and stale scenarios. Neither the two-sigma choice nor its operational desirability is established by the paper.

limitations: No CSVs were read, hashes verified or simulations rerun in this review. Replay success is supplied evidence of reproducibility, not an independently executed validation of the physical model.

Wilson intervals have approximate coverage. Bonferroni adjusts multiplicity but does not turn approximate marginal coverage into an exact finite-sample familywise guarantee; paired covariance is not exploited.

False-alert rates rise from 15.11% to 55.75% for fresh candidates and from 14.72% to 58.21% for stale candidates. These are conditional on nontransits, not fractions of alerts that are false; no operational loss function establishes an acceptable tradeoff.
Zero fresh misses among 897 true crossings does not establish zero population risk. The supplied treatment recall interval has a lower bound of approximately 98.54%.

Insufficient evidence establishes that residual stale misses are timing-related or more frequent in the underlying population than fresh misses. The summaries lack a spatial-versus-temporal failure decomposition.

The branches use different candidate samples and unequal accumulated sample sizes. Their summaries do not establish the proposed matched comparison of two-sigma versus three-sigma guards or the incremental benefit of the third sigma.

Independent Gaussian errors, quoted distances interpreted as standard deviations, bounded uniform candidate sampling and zenith circular-orbit geometry are experimental assumptions. Brightness, SGP4, historical TLEs and observational calibration are absent; baseline agreement is only a geometry consistency check.
The literature already suggests field expansion. This scoped sensitivity result establishes neither scientific novelty nor universality, full-paper reproduction or real-world predictive performance.
validation.reasoning: The supplied evidence supports the numerical goal for the fixed three-sigma recipe. Three distinct seed batches exceed the two-batch minimum; their reported replay counts total 7168 candidates. The contingency tables agree with the measurements: fresh misses decrease from 137/897 to 0/897, and stale misses from 112/880 to 2/880. Treatment-minus-control intervals are [-0.20165, -0.09933] and [-0.17367, -0.07260]; both lie below -0.05 and have widths below 0.25. The supplied recall bounds independently reproduce these difference bounds by endpoint subtraction. The implementation adjusts for three branches, eight planned looks, two groups and four endpoints, avoiding ordinary unadjusted repeated testing. All three deterministic geometry checks also meet their specified tolerances. Source grounding is explicit: seed, page 2 states, "The ﬁeld of view could be expanded by this distance and the results interpreted probabilistically." With timing identical in both arms, the nested spatial alert boundary explains recovery of 137 fresh and 110 stale crossings. This supports spatial recovery under the simulation assumptions, but does not identify the causes of the two residual stale misses. The substantial false-alert increase prevents interpreting the result as an established operational improvement.
